virals.name: The Iran Watcher
virals.hook:
Trump sees the Vance-led MOU as a costly strategic failure that gave the Islamic Republic billions in oil revenue and critical time to regroup.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Trump has privately criticized the June agreement and questioned whether it was a costly mistake. The White House denies that he regrets it.

The MOU lifted American pressure before the Islamic Republic delivered any irreversible concessions.

The United States began removing its naval blockade, authorized Iranian oil sales and offered access to frozen assets. In return, the regime promised further negotiations over its nuclear program and temporary commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian oil exports surged from approximately 65,000 barrels per day in May to 1.75 million barrels per day in June.

The regime exported more than 52 million barrels worth an estimated $4.5 billion, providing an immediate financial lifeline for the IRGC, its military programs and its proxy network.

Yet the Islamic Republic did not surrender its enriched uranium, dismantle its enrichment infrastructure or relinquish its leverage over Hormuz.

The MOU deferred those questions to future negotiations while establishing on-site downblending as the minimum possible treatment of the stockpile. The regime retained the material, the infrastructure and the ability to reverse course.

It also placed sanctions relief, frozen assets and a reconstruction package of at least $300 billion on the table before a final agreement had been secured.

The Islamic Republic took the economic relief and then returned to coercion.

The IRGC resumed attacks on commercial shipping, the Hormuz arrangement collapsed and the United States was forced to revoke the oil authorization and restore its blockade.

But the regime kept the billions of dollars, breathing room and time it had gained.

Vance was central to the diplomatic track. He helped negotiate the framework, led the talks and publicly defended the result.

The central failure was not diplomacy. It was sequencing.

The United States surrendered enforceable leverage before receiving enforceable concessions. The Islamic Republic monetized the pause, preserved its nuclear assets and resumed pressure after securing the immediate benefits.

The June MOU was presented as an off-ramp from war. In practice, it became an escape route for the Islamic Republic.

virals.name: The Iran Watcher
virals.hook:
The Islamic Republic has rejected transferring its stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium to Russia, deepening the fundamental divide with the United States and undermining prospects for a quick diplomatic breakthrough.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the regime’s Supreme National Security Council, stated:

“We informed our Russian friends that the enriched material will remain in Iran, and we will use it ourselves.”

The message is unambiguous. The Islamic Republic will not allow Russia to hold roughly 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent as part of a negotiated settlement.

Russia has repeatedly proposed taking custody of the material, similar to the arrangement used under the 2015 nuclear agreement. Removing it from Iran would create distance between the regime and a potential nuclear weapon while providing negotiators with an immediate confidence-building measure.

The Islamic Republic has refused.

Rezaei has repeated that no enriched material will leave Iran and claims the stockpile is needed for nuclear-powered ships and submarines. More importantly, the regime considers it strategic leverage that can be exchanged only for sweeping American concessions.

The statement also suggests the issue was raised through recent high-level discussions with Russia. Rezaei met Vladimir Putin in early November while carrying a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He has now publicly confirmed that Russia was told the stockpile will remain inside Iran.

This directly reinforces the Islamic Republic’s seven conditions.

The regime is demanding an end to hostilities across the region, the lifting of the American naval blockade, sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets, the withdrawal of American forces, war reparations and an end to external pressure.

Its sequencing is equally important.

The United States must satisfy or guarantee these conditions first. Only then will the Islamic Republic consider reopening the Strait of Hormuz and entering negotiations.

The nuclear issue would come afterward.

That is fundamentally incompatible with the American position.

President Trump has declared that the Islamic Republic will never be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon. Any serious agreement would therefore need to address the 60-percent stockpile, enrichment capacity and the regime’s ability to rapidly rebuild its program.

The Islamic Republic is instead demanding economic, military and strategic relief while retaining both its enriched uranium and Hormuz leverage.

That is not an offer to exchange nuclear restraint for sanctions relief. It is a demand that the United States surrender its pressure before the regime begins negotiating over the capabilities that created the crisis.

Qatar may have secured a two-week diplomatic window, but it has not narrowed the central disagreement.

The United States wants the nuclear threat reduced before surrendering leverage. The Islamic Republic wants American leverage dismantled before discussing the nuclear threat.

Rezaei’s statement shows that the regime is not preparing an early nuclear concession. It is preserving its most dangerous asset while demanding payment merely to enter negotiations.

Unless one side abandons its sequencing, the diplomatic window will delay the confrontation rather than resolve it.

virals.hook:

Senior IRGC adviser Mohammad Reza Naqdi said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the armed forces greater freedom of action and authorization to operate “in any geographical area.”

This expands the regime’s Mosaic Defense doctrine, a decentralized system designed to keep fighting if leaders are killed, command centres are destroyed or communications are cut.

The IRGC has divided Iran into provincial commands with their own leadership, intelligence networks, weapons, missile and drone stockpiles, and Basij forces.

Each command receives broad instructions in advance. If contact with central command is lost, regional commanders can select targets and continue attacking without waiting for new orders.

Senior positions also have designated replacements, allowing operations to continue after commanders are killed.

Naqdi’s statement expands that danger beyond the region.

The Islamic Republic has already threatened American bases across Europe. Regime officials have specifically warned that missiles could be fired toward European countries if their territory is used for American operations.

Under the expanded doctrine, regional forces could target European bases, international shipping and civilian infrastructure through missiles, drones, cyberattacks or overseas IRGC networks.

The Islamic Republic has created a military system designed to keep attacking without its head—and has now given that system worldwide reach.

The danger is that once central control disappears, multiple commanders may be able to expand the war into Europe while nobody retains the power to reliably order every armed unit to stop.

As an Iranian republican, not a monarchist, who firmly supports Prince Reza Pahlavi, I find your explanation completely unconvincing.

Your conduct at his press conference was highly unusual and, in my view, inappropriate. Having an obstructed view while filming does not automatically justify removing your shoes and sitting with your leg raised on a windowsill, particularly when other seating was available.

Have you ever removed your shoes, sat with one leg raised on a windowsill, and questioned a member of the British Royal Family in that posture? Or behaved similarly toward a British political leader at a formal press conference?

If not, why did you consider it appropriate when questioning Prince Reza Pahlavi?

Respect is not about royal privilege or social hierarchy. It is about applying the same standards of professional conduct to everyone.

Instead of spending your time defending your inappropriate conduct, start holding your own government accountable!

outsiders.hook:
شاهزاده رضا پهلوی در نشستی خبری در شهر کراکوف لهستان، در پاسخ به پرسش خبرنگار روزنامه «دیلی بریتین» درباره آینده خاورمیانه پس از سقوط جمهوری اسلامی و فروپاشی احتمالی سپاه پاسداران و نگرانی‌های بین‌المللی از خلاء قدرت مشابه عراق یا لیبی، تأکید کرد که این نگرانی‌ها عادلانه است.

وی با اشاره به لزوم جلوگیری از اشتباهات گذشته و تسهیل یک انتقال پایدار تصریح کرد که برای به حداقل رساندن مقاومت، باید به نیروها و بوروکرات‌های رژیم استراتژی خروج ارائه داد. شاهزاده رضا پهلوی افزود هر کسی که دستش به خون آلوده نباشد، در آینده جایگاه دارد و می‌تواند بخشی از راه‌حل باشد، در حالی که عاملان جنایات باید مسیر قانونی محاکماتی همچون نورنبرگ را طی کنند.

Maximum pressure plus maximum support can bring maximum defections from the regime. Footage of the reporter's informal posture drew criticism from many Iranian users.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
Trump sees the Vance-led MOU as a costly strategic failure that gave the Islamic Republic billions in oil revenue and critical time to regroup.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Trump has privately criticized the June agreement and questioned whether it was a costly mistake. The White House denies that he regrets it.

The MOU lifted American pressure before the Islamic Republic delivered any irreversible concessions.

The United States began removing its naval blockade, authorized Iranian oil sales and offered access to frozen assets. In return, the regime promised further negotiations over its nuclear program and temporary commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian oil exports surged from approximately 65,000 barrels per day in May to 1.75 million barrels per day in June.

The regime exported more than 52 million barrels worth an estimated $4.5 billion, providing an immediate financial lifeline for the IRGC, its military programs and its proxy network.

Yet the Islamic Republic did not surrender its enriched uranium, dismantle its enrichment infrastructure or relinquish its leverage over Hormuz.

The MOU deferred those questions to future negotiations while establishing on-site downblending as the minimum possible treatment of the stockpile. The regime retained the material, the infrastructure and the ability to reverse course.

It also placed sanctions relief, frozen assets and a reconstruction package of at least $300 billion on the table before a final agreement had been secured.

The Islamic Republic took the economic relief and then returned to coercion.

The IRGC resumed attacks on commercial shipping, the Hormuz arrangement collapsed and the United States was forced to revoke the oil authorization and restore its blockade.

But the regime kept the billions of dollars, breathing room and time it had gained.

Vance was central to the diplomatic track. He helped negotiate the framework, led the talks and publicly defended the result.

The central failure was not diplomacy. It was sequencing.

The United States surrendered enforceable leverage before receiving enforceable concessions. The Islamic Republic monetized the pause, preserved its nuclear assets and resumed pressure after securing the immediate benefits.

The June MOU was presented as an off-ramp from war. In practice, it became an escape route for the Islamic Republic.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
The Islamic Republic has rejected transferring its stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium to Russia, deepening the fundamental divide with the United States and undermining prospects for a quick diplomatic breakthrough.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the regime’s Supreme National Security Council, stated:

“We informed our Russian friends that the enriched material will remain in Iran, and we will use it ourselves.”

The message is unambiguous. The Islamic Republic will not allow Russia to hold roughly 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent as part of a negotiated settlement.

Russia has repeatedly proposed taking custody of the material, similar to the arrangement used under the 2015 nuclear agreement. Removing it from Iran would create distance between the regime and a potential nuclear weapon while providing negotiators with an immediate confidence-building measure.

The Islamic Republic has refused.

Rezaei has repeated that no enriched material will leave Iran and claims the stockpile is needed for nuclear-powered ships and submarines. More importantly, the regime considers it strategic leverage that can be exchanged only for sweeping American concessions.

The statement also suggests the issue was raised through recent high-level discussions with Russia. Rezaei met Vladimir Putin in early November while carrying a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He has now publicly confirmed that Russia was told the stockpile will remain inside Iran.

This directly reinforces the Islamic Republic’s seven conditions.

The regime is demanding an end to hostilities across the region, the lifting of the American naval blockade, sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets, the withdrawal of American forces, war reparations and an end to external pressure.

Its sequencing is equally important.

The United States must satisfy or guarantee these conditions first. Only then will the Islamic Republic consider reopening the Strait of Hormuz and entering negotiations.

The nuclear issue would come afterward.

That is fundamentally incompatible with the American position.

President Trump has declared that the Islamic Republic will never be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon. Any serious agreement would therefore need to address the 60-percent stockpile, enrichment capacity and the regime’s ability to rapidly rebuild its program.

The Islamic Republic is instead demanding economic, military and strategic relief while retaining both its enriched uranium and Hormuz leverage.

That is not an offer to exchange nuclear restraint for sanctions relief. It is a demand that the United States surrender its pressure before the regime begins negotiating over the capabilities that created the crisis.

Qatar may have secured a two-week diplomatic window, but it has not narrowed the central disagreement.

The United States wants the nuclear threat reduced before surrendering leverage. The Islamic Republic wants American leverage dismantled before discussing the nuclear threat.

Rezaei’s statement shows that the regime is not preparing an early nuclear concession. It is preserving its most dangerous asset while demanding payment merely to enter negotiations.

Unless one side abandons its sequencing, the diplomatic window will delay the confrontation rather than resolve it.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
President Trump says the Islamic Republic has waged war against America since 1979 - and is now facing the consequences of the confrontation it started.

“America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.”

The Islamic Republic declared America its enemy, killed hundreds of Americans and spent 47 years creating the confrontation that may now bring down the regime.

The historical record supports the core of that argument.

The regime’s hostility was not a reaction to one sanction, military strike or failed negotiation. It was embedded in its founding ideology.

Ayatollah Khomeini called the United States the “Great Satan” and made exporting the Islamic Revolution a central mission. Ali Khamenei continued that doctrine, using proxies, terrorism, missiles and nuclear leverage to confront America and remove its influence from the region.

The Islamic Republic began its rule by seizing the U.S. Embassy and holding 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.

It then helped create Hezbollah through the IRGC and transformed proxy warfare into state policy.

Bombings of the American embassy and Marine barracks in Lebanon killed 258 Americans in 1983. Americans were later kidnapped, tortured and murdered by groups within the regime’s network. The 1996 Khobar Towers bombing killed another 19 American airmen.

But the regime’s hostility must never be confused with the Iranian people.

After the September 11 attacks, thousands of ordinary Iranians in Tehran and other cities held candlelight vigils in solidarity with the American people.

That response exposed the divide between Iranians capable of compassion toward Americans and a regime that portrayed America as an eternal enemy.

The Islamic Republic’s most sustained campaign against American forces came in Iraq.

Under Qassem Soleimani, the IRGC armed, trained and directed militias that attacked Americans with rockets, mortars and explosively formed penetrators supplied through Iranian networks.

The United States assessed that Iran-backed militants killed at least 603 American personnel in Iraq—approximately one in every six American deaths during the war.

The regime denied responsibility while its officials and media celebrated the damage inflicted by its militias.

That deniability was deliberate.

Proxies allowed the Islamic Republic to kill Americans, destabilize neighbouring countries and expand the IRGC’s power while attempting to avoid direct retaliation.

The campaign survived both Supreme Leaders and continued across multiple American administrations.

In 2020, the Islamic Republic directly launched ballistic missiles at American bases, leaving more than 100 personnel with traumatic brain injuries. Its proxies continued attacking American forces across Iraq, Syria and Jordan.

The campaign also reached American soil.

U.S. authorities charged IRGC-linked operatives over plots to assassinate Donald Trump and former officials involved in the Soleimani strike, including John Bolton and Mike Pompeo.

Islamic Republic media broadcast threats against Trump’s family. IRGC-linked operatives plotted against U.S. politicians including Donald Trump, Joe Biden, and Nikki Haley. 

The regime also directed repeated attempts to kidnap or murder Iranian-American dissident Masih Alinejad, conducted surveillance of regime critics in the United States and Western allied countries, and recruited individuals inside the United States to collect sensitive information.

These were not merely angry statements. They resulted in disrupted operations, criminal charges and convictions.

This was never a temporary dispute between two governments. Hostage-taking, terrorism, proxy warfare and assassination plots became permanent instruments of Islamic Republic policy.

The regime believed it could wage an undeclared war indefinitely while keeping the consequences away from Iran.

That strategy produced tactical gains but became a strategic disaster for the country.

The Islamic Republic sacrificed Iran’s economy, security and international standing to sustain an ideological war the Iranian people never chose.

It spent Iran’s wealth on militias, missiles and nuclear leverage while the country’s infrastructure deteriorated and its people became poorer.

The Islamic Republic used America as a permanent enemy to defend its rule at home.

It may now discover that the enemy it spent 47 years provoking has become the force capable of ending it.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
The Islamic Republic confirms regional military commanders can attack worldwide without central approval, with Europe explicitly in their sights.

Senior IRGC adviser Mohammad Reza Naqdi said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the armed forces greater freedom of action and authorization to operate “in any geographical area.”

This expands the regime’s Mosaic Defense doctrine, a decentralized system designed to keep fighting if leaders are killed, command centres are destroyed or communications are cut.

The IRGC has divided Iran into provincial commands with their own leadership, intelligence networks, weapons, missile and drone stockpiles, and Basij forces.

Each command receives broad instructions in advance. If contact with central command is lost, regional commanders can select targets and continue attacking without waiting for new orders.

Senior positions also have designated replacements, allowing operations to continue after commanders are killed.

The system was tested during the intensive 40-day phase of the 2026 war. Despite the deaths of Ali Khamenei, the IRGC commander and other senior figures, missile and drone attacks continued because authority had already been distributed.

The strategy makes the Islamic Republic harder to disable—but also harder to control.

Once communications collapse, central leaders may not know what every unit is doing or possess the ability to stop them. Regional commanders can misinterpret broad orders, attack unintended targets or trigger a wider war.

Naqdi’s statement expands that danger beyond the region.

The Islamic Republic has already threatened American bases across Europe. Regime officials have specifically warned that missiles could be fired toward European countries if their territory is used for American operations.

Under the expanded doctrine, regional forces could target European bases, international shipping and civilian infrastructure through missiles, drones, cyberattacks or overseas IRGC networks.

The Islamic Republic has created a military system designed to keep attacking without its head—and has now given that system worldwide reach.

The danger is that once central control disappears, multiple commanders may be able to expand the war into Europe while nobody retains the power to reliably order every armed unit to stop.

outsiders.name: Moh Heidari
outsiders.hook:
David @daveatherton 

As an Iranian republican, not a monarchist, who firmly supports Prince Reza Pahlavi, I find your explanation completely unconvincing.

Your conduct at his press conference was highly unusual and, in my view, inappropriate. Having an obstructed view while filming does not automatically justify removing your shoes and sitting with your leg raised on a windowsill, particularly when other seating was available.

You invoke British cultural norms and equality. But equality does not mean abandoning basic professional courtesy.

Have you ever removed your shoes, sat with one leg raised on a windowsill, and questioned a member of the British Royal Family in that posture? Or behaved similarly toward a British political leader at a formal press conference?

If not, why did you consider it appropriate when questioning Prince Reza Pahlavi?

Respect is not about royal privilege or social hierarchy. It is about applying the same standards of professional conduct to everyone.

And since you brought up the IRGC, here’s a far more consequential challenge for you as a British journalist:

Instead of spending your time defending your inappropriate conduct, start holding your own government accountable!

For decades, what access to Britain has been granted to senior officials of the Islamic Republic, IRGC commanders, and members of the regime’s ruling families, including Mojtaba Khamenei?

Demand that British authorities including British intelligence agencies to disclose who received visas or entry permission, the dates of issuance, who authorized them, and on what legal grounds!

Investigate whether politically connected individuals associated with a regime accused of grave human rights abuses have benefited from British immigration decisions, and demand answers from the politicians responsible.

I acknowledge your stated support for the Iranian people’s struggle for freedom. But supporting that struggle does not exempt anyone from legitimate criticism or professional accountability.

If you genuinely want to challenge the IRGC and the Islamic Republic, put your journalistic influence to work investigating the decisions of your own government. That would be a far more meaningful contribution to the cause of Iranian freedom than turning a serious press conference into a spectacle.

ideas.angle: Turn the UN vote outrage into a single shareable number card and name the countries that voted no.
ideas.hook_en: 144 countries just helped the Islamic Republic onto a United Nations committee. 39 said no. The Iranian regime hangs protesters and still gets a seat.
ideas.why: Canada FM Anita Anand's post against the seat drew 49.8K views and realMaalouf's post on the vote 45.6K; Islamic Republic is #2 on the X keyword sample (125.7K vs 66.6K prior 24h).

ideas.title: Thank you, Canada
ideas.visual: 15s vertical clip: Anand's post on screen, cut to diaspora rally footage with lion-and-sun flags, EN captions.
ideas.angle: Positive reinforcement post: thank Canada for voting no and push other democracies to follow.
ideas.hook_en: Canada voted no on giving the Iranian regime a UN seat and said it stands with the people of Iran. Free Iran needs more governments willing to say that out loud.
ideas.why: Anita Anand's post hit 49.8K views and UN Watch / Iran International amplified it; Free Iran jumped to 111.7K on the X keyword sample vs 1.3K the prior 24h.

ideas.title: Exit door or Nuremberg
ideas.visual: 3-slide carousel: 1) 'Clean hands? There is a place for you.' 2) 'Blood on your hands? Court.' 3) Krakow press-conference photo of the Crown Prince.
ideas.angle: Explain the Crown Prince's transition plan as a two-door choice for IRGC and regime personnel.
ideas.hook_en: The Crown Prince's message to IRGC and Iranian regime staff is simple: clean hands, a future in a free Iran. Blood on your hands, a courtroom.
ideas.why: indypersian's Krakow press-conference report drew 72.2K views; IRGC is steady on the X keyword sample (24K vs 20K).

ideas.title: The MOU lifeline
ideas.visual: Simple bar chart image: Iranian oil exports May vs June as reported (65,000 vs 1.75 million barrels/day), source line citing the post.
ideas.angle: Use the reported oil-export jump to argue that easing pressure funds the IRGC.
ideas.hook_en: Ease the pressure and the Islamic Republic cashes in: oil exports went from about 65,000 to 1.75 million barrels a day, per TheIranWatcher. Guess who got the money - the IRGC.
ideas.why: TheIranWatcher's MOU post (citing WSJ) drew 67K views; Islamic Republic is up on the X keyword sample.

ideas.title: 10 months, still counting
ideas.visual: 30-45s memorial montage with candles, names and faces from the January uprising, EN captions and date stamp.
ideas.angle: Keep the January massacre anniversary in front of English audiences while the memorial video is still climbing.
ideas.hook_en: 10 months since the massacre. The Iranian people have not forgotten a single name. Woman Life Freedom was never a slogan, it was a promise.
ideas.why: IranianPlateau's memorial video climbed to 158.8K views (from 82.6K yesterday), the only Iran-core watchlist hit; Woman Life Freedom rose to 8.5K vs 1K on the X keyword sample.

ideas.title: Hitler's unfinished work
ideas.visual: 20s clip of the Crown Prince at Auschwitz-Birkenau with Yasmine Pahlavi, burned-in EN subtitles of the 'finish Hitler's unfinished work' line.
ideas.angle: Re-cut the Auschwitz line for English audiences: a regime that denies the Holocaust while threatening another.
ideas.hook_en: At Auschwitz, Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi warned the regime in Tehran wants to finish what Hitler started. The Holocaust deniers ruling Iran do not speak for Iranians.
ideas.why: rangoooo_'s post of the quote drew 74.3K views and PahlaviComms' Auschwitz post 42K; Pahlavi is rising on the X keyword sample (20.8K vs 15.6K).

x_keywords.method: Read-only x MCP search_posts_all, 2 calls per keyword: last 24 h and previous 24 h (24-48 h ago); lang:en, no retweets/replies, sort=relevancy, up to 25 posts per window. This is a SAMPLE of top-relevance posts, not every post on X. Views = impression_count at fetch time. Rank = sum of sampled 24 h views; 48 h = both windows; trend = 24 h sum / previous 24 h sum (up >=1.3, down <=0.7). Fresh posts are still gaining views, so 'up' is understated. Top-post share > 70% means one viral post carries the keyword.

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
